title: I Am Joseph Your Brother
summary: Joseph reveals himself to his terrified brothers, forgives them, declares that God sent him ahead to preserve life, and sends for Jacob, whose spirit revives.
historicalContext: Twenty-two years separate the seventeen-year-old dreamer of chapter 37 from the thirty-nine-year-old vizier who now speaks to his brothers (41:46; 45:6). Two years of the seven-year famine have passed, and the failure of the Nile flood has left Egypt and its neighbours dependent on the grain Joseph stored. Joseph’s offices are described in terms that suit a high Egyptian official: counsellor to the king, master of the royal household, and ruler over the land. Goshen lay in the eastern Delta, well watered and suited to herds, and close enough to the seat of government that Joseph could keep his family near him. Wheeled carts were uncommon among the herdsmen of Canaan’s hill country, which helps explain why the Egyptian wagons became the decisive proof for Jacob. Hebron, where Jacob had long camped (37:14), was the home to which the brothers carried the news.
literaryContext: Genesis 45 is the turning point of the whole Joseph story. Judah’s offer to become a slave in place of Benjamin (44:18-34) shows that the brothers who sold Joseph have changed, and Joseph can no longer keep up the disguise. The chapter falls into two movements. In the first (vv. 1-15) Joseph alone speaks, and his speech is framed by weeping; at its centre stands the threefold declaration that God sent him, which supplies the theological key to chapters 37-50 and anticipates 50:20. In the second (vv. 16-28) the scene widens to Pharaoh’s court and then to Canaan, as royal invitation, generous gifts, and the long journey bring the news to Jacob. The chapter reverses earlier scenes: brothers who could not speak peaceably to Joseph now talk with him (37:4; 45:15), new garments replace the stripped robe, and a father who believed a lie about a death must now believe the truth about a life.
themes: Providence overruling human sin without excusing it
Forgiveness offered by the one who was wronged
A remnant preserved for the promise
Generous provision for the whole family
Hope revived by the word and visible tokens

outline.title: Joseph Makes Himself Known
outline.summary: Unable to hold back, Joseph clears the room, weeps aloud, and declares himself to his speechless brothers, inviting them to come near.

outline.title: God Sent Me Before You
outline.summary: Joseph tells his brothers not to torment themselves, for God overruled their sin and sent him ahead to preserve life and keep a remnant alive.

outline.title: Come Down to Me
outline.summary: Joseph urges them to bring Jacob quickly to Goshen where he will provide for them, then embraces Benjamin and kisses all his brothers, who at last talk with him.

outline.title: Pharaoh’s Welcome and Joseph’s Gifts
outline.summary: Pharaoh gladly invites the family and sends wagons; Joseph adds provisions, garments, silver, and gifts for his father, and warns his brothers not to quarrel.

outline.title: Jacob’s Spirit Revived
outline.summary: Jacob at first cannot believe the news, but Joseph’s words and the wagons revive him, and Israel resolves to go and see his son before he dies.

verses.bibleText: Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me. And there stood no man with him, while Joseph made himself known unto his brethren.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah’s plea ended on the words “my father” and the picture of an old man going down to the grave in grief (44:34). The brother who had once proposed selling Joseph for silver was now offering himself as a slave so that Rachel’s other son could go home. Whatever Joseph had hoped to learn through his long testing was now plain: the brothers who had shrugged at their father’s anguish over a bloodied coat would rather suffer than see that anguish again. The narrator says simply that Joseph “could not refrain himself.” Twice before he had turned away to weep in private (42:24; 43:30-31), and twice he had recovered his composure. This time the restraint gives way.

His first act is to clear the room. “Cause every man to go out from me” is an order to the Egyptian attendants, the steward among them, who had carried out the plan with the silver cup. What follows belongs to the family alone. Joseph is about to name the sale at Dothan, and to speak of it before strangers would shame his brothers; sending the servants away spares them public disgrace before a word of pardon has been spoken. The command also shows where Joseph’s heart lies. For years he has worn Egyptian linen, carried an Egyptian name, and spoken through an interpreter. Now he shuts the court out and stands alone with the shepherds of Canaan.

“While Joseph made himself known unto his brethren” summarizes the scene that follows. The verb is reflexive: Joseph discloses himself, and the brothers can know him only because he chooses to be known. Stephen recalls the moment before the council: “at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren” (Acts 7:13), placing it in a pattern where Israel’s deliverers are first refused and afterward recognized. Christian readers think of the risen Lord, who was known to his disciples only when he opened their eyes (Luke 24:31), and whose self-disclosure, like Joseph’s, came as grace to those who had failed him.

wordNotes.term: לְהִתְאַפֵּק (lehit’appeq) — to refrain himself
wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form meaning to hold oneself in or keep control. The same verb described Joseph washing his face and mastering himself after weeping in his chamber (43:31). Now he cannot. The verb is used of God as well, who says he has long “refrained” himself before acting to save his people (Isaiah 42:14), so restraint that finally gives way can be the moment love acts.

wordNotes.term: בְּהִתְוַדַּע (behitwadda‘) — while he made himself known
wordNotes.explanation: A rare reflexive form of yada‘, “to know.” Its only other occurrence describes the LORD making himself known to a prophet in a vision (Numbers 12:6). The form stresses that the revelation comes from the one revealed; the brothers did not discover Joseph, he disclosed himself to them. Stephen’s retelling uses the corresponding Greek passive, “was made known” (Acts 7:13).

verses.bibleText: And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Literally, Joseph “gave his voice in weeping.” This is no quiet tear but loud, unrestrained crying, so loud that the Egyptians just sent out of the room heard it, and word of it reached “the house of Pharaoh.” The text need not mean that the sound carried to the palace itself; the servants outside heard, and the report travelled. Verse 16 picks up the same thread when “the fame thereof was heard in Pharaoh’s house.”

Joseph weeps more often than anyone else in Genesis (42:24; 43:30; 45:14-15; 46:29; 50:1, 17). His tears tell the reader what his stern words had hidden: the harshness of the earlier meetings was never revenge. In a court that prized composure, the most capable man in Egypt sobs without shame over the brothers who sold him. Scripture does not treat such tears as weakness. Jesus wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35), and believers are told to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). Grief and love held back for twenty-two years now break out together.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתֵּן אֶת־קֹלוֹ בִּבְכִי (vayyitten et-qolo bivkhi) — he wept aloud
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “he gave his voice in weeping,” an idiom for loud, audible crying. Similar expressions describe Hagar lifting up her voice beside her dying son (21:16), Esau’s cry when the blessing was lost (27:38), and Israel weeping through the night after the spies’ report (Numbers 14:1). Here the outcry comes not from loss but from love that can no longer be hidden.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto his brethren, I am Joseph; doth my father yet live? And his brethren could not answer him; for they were troubled at his presence.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I am Joseph” is only two words in Hebrew, and Joseph speaks them in his brothers’ own language, without the interpreter who had stood between them (42:23). The last time they had spoken that name together was over a goat-stained coat held out to their father with a lie: “know now whether it be thy son’s coat or no” (37:32). The voice and face of the lord of Egypt suddenly take on the features of the boy in the pit.

His first question is about Jacob: “doth my father yet live?” He had asked before and been told (43:27-28), and Judah’s whole speech presupposed the old man was alive. But earlier Joseph had spoken coolly of “your father, the old man of whom ye spake.” Now he says “my father.” Judah’s repeated references to “thy servant our father” had stirred the son beneath the Egyptian official, and the question comes out of longing more than any need for information.

The brothers “could not answer him.” The narrator sets their silence beside Joseph’s loss of control: he could not refrain, and they could not speak. They “were troubled at his presence,” a word for alarm that paralyses. They had confessed among themselves that their distress was payment for what they did to Joseph (42:21), but they had feared God’s hand, not their brother’s. Now they stand in the power of the very man they stripped and sold, with no idea what he intends. Guilt makes the presence of the wronged one terrifying, as Adam hid from the voice of God in the garden (3:8-10). The answer to that terror does not lie in the brothers. It must come from the one they wronged, and the next verses give it.

wordNotes.term: נִבְהֲלוּ (nivhalu) — they were troubled
wordNotes.explanation: From bahal, sudden dismay or terror that leaves a person shaken and helpless. It describes the chiefs of Edom trembling at Israel’s deliverance (Exodus 15:15), the men of Benjamin when they saw disaster upon them (Judges 20:41), and Saul collapsing before the woman at Endor (1 Samuel 28:21). The brothers feel more than embarrassment; they are struck with fear for their lives.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you. And they came near. And he said, I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers have shrunk back, so Joseph closes the distance with an invitation: “Come near to me, I pray you.” The ruler of Egypt does not command; he asks. “And they came near.” Their first step toward reconciliation is simply obeying the call of the one they had wronged, and that obedience costs them their fear.

Then he repeats his identity with a detail no impostor could know: “I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.” Only the ten and Joseph himself knew what had happened at Dothan. The words prove who he is, and they also name the sin without softening it. Joseph does not pretend the past never happened; forgiveness that refuses to speak of the wrong is not forgiveness at all. Yet the order of his words matters. “Your brother” comes first, and only then “whom ye sold.” The relationship is affirmed before the offence is mentioned, and the offence is mentioned only so that it can be dealt with. Joseph does not hold the sale over their heads or demand an explanation. He states the fact once, and in the next breath he will begin to lift its weight. There is a painful echo here: when Judah urged the sale, his argument was “he is our brother and our flesh” (37:27). They had sold a brother; the brother now claims them.

The Christian reader will hear in this scene the gospel’s call. The Son of God is “not ashamed to call them brethren” (Hebrews 2:11), even though it was human sin that brought him to suffering, and those who were far off are “made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). The way back to God begins, as it did for these brothers, with the voice of the injured one saying, “Come near.”

wordNotes.term: גְּשׁוּ־נָא אֵלַי (geshu-na elay) — come near to me, I pray you
wordNotes.explanation: The verb nagash means to approach or draw close, and the particle na turns the command into a gentle request. Judah had “come near” to plead before Joseph (44:18); now Joseph invites all of them. Earlier blind Isaac had said to Jacob, “Come near now,” in a scene of deception (27:21); here drawing near leads to truth and pardon. The same idea of approach underlies the invitation to draw near to God with a true heart (Hebrews 10:22).

verses.bibleText: Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph can see on his brothers’ faces that terror is turning into self-reproach, and he speaks to it at once: “Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves.” The two verbs describe pain and a burning anger turned inward, the same pair used when Jacob’s sons heard what had been done to Dinah (34:7). Joseph does not deny what they did. In the same breath he repeats it: “that ye sold me hither.” Then comes the sentence on which the whole Joseph story turns: “for God did send me before you to preserve life.”

Two actors stand behind one event. The brothers sold; God sent. Their purpose was to be rid of a dreamer and see what would become of his dreams (37:20). God’s purpose was life. Neither cancels the other. The sale remains a sin, and the brothers have already owned it as such (42:21; 44:16). It is to men who have confessed and changed that Joseph offers this comfort. The same words spoken to unrepentant men would have made sin cheap; spoken to the penitent, they lift a weight that God himself has removed. Scripture holds the two truths together elsewhere: Jesus was “delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,” and yet taken “by wicked hands” (Acts 2:23). God is not the author of evil, but he is never its prisoner. He takes what people mean for harm and makes it serve his saving design, as Joseph will say again at their father’s death (50:20).

“To preserve life” is broad. The grain Joseph gathered fed Egypt and “all countries” that came to buy (41:57); the blessing promised through Abraham’s seed is reaching the nations (12:3). Verse 7 will narrow the focus to the family itself.

Peter’s preaching in Jerusalem follows the same shape: you denied and killed the Prince of life, God fulfilled what he had foretold, therefore repent (Acts 3:14-19). The rejected brother became the means of salvation for those who rejected him. Joseph’s words also guard against misuse. He speaks of his own suffering, from the far side of it, after God has shown him the outcome. He offers no formula for telling the wounded that their wounds were good.

wordNotes.term: אַל־תֵּעָצְבוּ (al-te‘atsevu) — be not grieved
wordNotes.explanation: From ‘atsav, to be hurt or pained. It is joined here with a phrase meaning literally “let it not burn in your eyes,” that is, do not be angry with yourselves. The same pairing describes Dinah’s brothers (34:7) and Jonathan when he learned his father meant to kill David (1 Samuel 20:34). Joseph does not forbid sorrow for sin; he forbids the self-torment that would go on punishing what has been forgiven. Paul distinguishes godly sorrow that leads to repentance from sorrow that works death (2 Corinthians 7:10).

wordNotes.term: לְמִחְיָה (lemichyah) — to preserve life
wordNotes.explanation: The noun michyah refers to what keeps a person alive. It can mean food and sustenance, as when the Midianites left Israel “no sustenance” (Judges 6:4), or a reviving, as when Ezra thanks God for “a little reviving” in bondage (Ezra 9:8). Joseph was sent to be the means by which life would be sustained in famine.

verses.bibleText: For these two years hath the famine been in the land: and yet there are five years, in the which there shall neither be earing nor harvest.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph explains the urgency. The famine has lasted two years, and five more remain “in the which there shall neither be earing nor harvest.” “Earing” is an old English word for ploughing, so the phrase means that the whole farming cycle will fail. Since Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (41:46) and seven years of plenty followed, he is now about thirty-nine.

The statement is general rather than absolute; later the Egyptians ask Joseph for seed to sow (47:19), so some planting went on near the river. But no one could expect a normal harvest. Joseph knows the future length of the famine only because God revealed it through Pharaoh’s dreams (41:25-32), and that knowledge itself is a sign of God at work. For the family in Canaan, the conclusion is unavoidable: if they stay where they are, they will be ruined before the famine ends.

The warning also shows the mercy behind God’s dealings. He did not let the famine fall without notice. Seven years before the first failed harvest he told Pharaoh what was coming and placed a man ready to act on it. the Lord reveals “his secret unto his servants” (Amos 3:7). The same God who sent the warning now sends the invitation, and Joseph’s five remaining years become a reason to move rather than a cause for despair.

wordNotes.term: חָרִישׁ וְקָצִיר (charish veqatsir) — earing and harvest
wordNotes.explanation: Ploughing and reaping, the start and end of the agricultural year, together stand for the whole of farming. The same pair appears in the Sabbath commandment of Exodus 34:21: “in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest,” where even the busiest seasons may not crowd out the seventh day. The verb behind charish is used of ploughing a king’s fields in 1 Samuel 8:12.

verses.bibleText: And God sent me before you to preserve you a posterity in the earth, and to save your lives by a great deliverance.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
For the second time Joseph says that “God sent me before you,” and now he states the purpose in terms of the family: “to preserve you a posterity in the earth, and to save your lives by a great deliverance.” The word translated “posterity” means a remnant, what is left over after disaster. The word rendered “deliverance” refers to those who escape. Together they picture a small company carried safely through a catastrophe so that a future remains.

Much more than the survival of one household is at stake. The promise to Abraham, that his seed would become a great nation and bring blessing to all families of the earth (12:2-3; 22:17-18), depended on these seventy people. If Jacob’s family had starved in Canaan, the line from which Judah’s royal descendant would come (49:10) would have ended. The famine threatened the promise itself, much as the flood once threatened humanity until God preserved Noah’s household. In both cases God kept a remnant, and in both the rescue was his doing.

The two words Joseph uses later became part of the prophets’ vocabulary of hope. Isaiah speaks of a remnant that escapes and returns to the mighty God (Isaiah 10:20-21), and of a remnant going forth from Jerusalem and those who escape from Mount Zion (Isaiah 37:31-32). Joel promises deliverance in Mount Zion for whoever calls on the name of the LORD (Joel 2:32). Paul writes that “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5). The deliverance Joseph announces is “great,” beyond human contriving. It foreshadows the greater rescue God would bring through the promised Seed, who was sent ahead of his people through suffering to save many lives (Galatians 3:16; Hebrews 2:10).

wordNotes.term: שְׁאֵרִית (she’erit) — posterity (remnant)
wordNotes.explanation: From sha’ar, “to remain,” the word denotes what survives a disaster and carries life forward. The KJV renders it “posterity” because the survivors here will become the future nation. The same word describes the remnant of Judah that would take root downward and bear fruit upward after the Assyrian crisis (2 Kings 19:30-31). Paul applies the idea to those whom grace preserves (Romans 11:5).

wordNotes.term: פְּלֵיטָה גְּדֹלָה (peletah gedolah) — a great deliverance
wordNotes.explanation: Peletah means an escape or a band of survivors. With she’erit it forms a fixed pair for those God rescues from judgment (Ezra 9:14). Joel promises that in Mount Zion “shall be deliverance” for all who call on the LORD (Joel 2:32), and Obadiah uses the same word for the escaped remnant on Zion (Obadiah 1:17). “Great” marks the rescue as something only God could accomplish.

verses.bibleText: So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God: and he hath made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house, and a ruler throughout all the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God.” For the third time Joseph names God as the one who sent him, and this time he sets the statement in the sharpest possible form. Read alone, it might sound as though the brothers bore no responsibility. But Joseph has just said twice that they sold him (vv. 4-5), and he will later tell them plainly that they “thought evil” against him (50:20). Hebrew often states relative weight by an absolute contrast. When Moses told the grumbling Israelites, “your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD” (Exodus 16:8), he did not mean that he and Aaron had not been murmured against; he meant that the real offence was against God. When the LORD told Samuel, “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me” (1 Samuel 8:7), Samuel had in fact been rejected. In the same way Joseph declares where the decisive cause and the final meaning of his journey lie. The brothers acted, and were guilty for it; God overruled, and his purpose determined the outcome.

This does not make God the source of their envy. God “tempteth no man” (James 1:13). He permitted their sin, set limits to it, and wove it into a design they could not see. Joseph’s faith rests in that larger hand, and it frees him from bitterness.

Joseph then describes what God has made him, using three titles. “A father to Pharaoh” portrays a trusted counsellor and provider for the king, as Eliakim was to be “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 22:21) and Job “a father to the poor” (Job 29:16). Egyptian court language had similar honorifics, but Joseph speaks as a Hebrew to Hebrews. “Lord of all his house” repeats Pharaoh’s own appointment (41:40), and “a ruler throughout all the land of Egypt” recalls Joseph’s public installation (41:43). That last word has a history. When Joseph first told his dreams, his brothers asked scornfully, “shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?” (37:8). God has now answered their question.

The pattern reaches its fullest meaning in Christ. The stone the builders refused has become the head of the corner (Psalm 118:22; Acts 4:11), and God has exalted the one whom his own people delivered up “to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins” (Acts 5:31).

wordNotes.term: לְאָב לְפַרְעֹה (le’av lefar‘oh) — a father to Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: “Father” here describes a senior adviser and protector rather than a family tie. Isaiah uses the same language for Eliakim, the steward who would be “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 22:21), and Job calls himself “a father to the poor” (Job 29:16). The title points to wisdom, care, and authority exercised on behalf of others. Joseph’s position was a trust given for the sake of many lives.

wordNotes.term: מֹשֵׁל (moshel) — ruler
wordNotes.explanation: A participle of mashal, “to rule, have dominion.” The brothers had mocked Joseph’s dream with the same verb: “shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?” (37:8). The psalmist recalls that God made Joseph “ruler of all his substance” (Psalm 105:21). Micah later promises a ruler in Israel from Bethlehem whose goings forth are from of old (Micah 5:2), the greater Son in whom such rule becomes salvation.

verses.bibleText: Haste ye, and go up to my father, and say unto him, Thus saith thy son Joseph, God hath made me lord of all Egypt: come down unto me, tarry not:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph turns from explanation to instruction, and his first word is “Haste ye.” The famine will not wait, Jacob is old, and Joseph has waited twenty-two years already. The message they are to carry is framed like a herald’s announcement: “Thus saith thy son Joseph.” Its first clause puts God at the front: “God hath made me lord of all Egypt.” Jacob had refused to be comforted for his son (37:35), and nothing would move him more than learning that the God of his fathers had been at work all along in the years of silence.

Then comes the summons: “come down unto me, tarry not.” Joseph anticipates hesitation. Jacob had clung to Benjamin and released him only under the pressure of hunger (42:38; 43:11-14), and he would have reason to fear leaving the land God promised. Abraham’s descent into Egypt had led to trouble (12:10-20), and Isaac had been forbidden to go there (26:2). Those doubts will be answered by God himself at Beersheba (46:3-4). For now the brothers must go quickly with news that changes everything.

The phrase “thy son Joseph” deserves notice. The lord of all Egypt, honoured by Pharaoh and feared by nations, introduces himself to Jacob first of all as a son. Rank and titles come second. His glory will be reported (v. 13), but the heart of the message is that the boy Jacob lost is still his child and longs for him. The brothers who once brought Jacob a coat and asked whether it was his son’s now bring him his son’s own words.

The pattern of hurried good news recurs in Scripture. The women at the empty tomb were told, “go quickly, and tell his disciples that he is risen” (Matthew 28:7). Joseph’s message, like theirs, announces that the one thought dead is alive and reigning, and it calls the hearers to come to him.

wordNotes.term: מַהֲרוּ … אַל־תַּעֲמֹד (maharu … al-ta‘amod) — haste ye … tarry not
wordNotes.explanation: Mahar means to hurry, and it opens and closes this part of Joseph’s speech (vv. 9, 13), giving the whole message a note of urgency. Abraham “hastened” to prepare food for his heavenly visitors (18:6). “Tarry not” is literally “do not stand still.” The same urgency marks the angel’s charge to the women at the tomb to go quickly with the news of the resurrection (Matthew 28:7).

verses.bibleText: And thou shalt dwell in the land of Goshen, and thou shalt be near unto me, thou, and thy children, and thy children's children, and thy flocks, and thy herds, and all that thou hast:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph has already chosen a place: “thou shalt dwell in the land of Goshen.” Goshen lay in the eastern Nile Delta, generally identified with the region around the Wadi Tumilat, a fertile strip suited to flocks and herds. It was good pasture, and it lay on the side of Egypt nearest Canaan. Later chapters show its other advantages. Shepherds were “an abomination unto the Egyptians” (46:34), so a separate district let Israel keep its own identity instead of dissolving into Egyptian society. And when judgment fell on Egypt in the days of Moses, God set Goshen apart so that no swarms of flies would be there (Exodus 8:22).

“Thou shalt be near unto me.” Joseph wants his family close, within reach of his care and his company. The list that follows is complete: Jacob, his children, his grandchildren, his flocks, his herds, “and all that thou hast.” Joseph is thinking in generations. He promises Goshen before consulting Pharaoh, which suggests how much authority over the land had been placed in his hands (41:40-41), though the king will soon add his own warm approval (vv. 16-20; 47:5-6). This district will become the nursery in which the family grows into a people that “increased abundantly, and multiplied” (Exodus 1:7).

The promise of a place near the one who saved them sounds a note heard again in the words of Jesus: “I go to prepare a place for you … that where I am, there ye may be also” (John 14:2-3). Joseph could give his family pasture through a famine; Christ promises his people a home in his presence.

wordNotes.term: גֹּשֶׁן (Goshen) — Goshen
wordNotes.explanation: A district of the eastern Delta, distinct from the town and region of the same name in southern Judah (Joshua 10:41; 15:51). Joseph’s family would be settled there because it was good grazing land (47:6), and it served to keep the shepherd family apart from Egyptian society (46:34). During the plagues it became the place God protected (Exodus 8:22; 9:26).

verses.bibleText: And there will I nourish thee; for yet there are five years of famine; lest thou, and thy household, and all that thou hast, come to poverty.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And there will I nourish thee; for yet there are five years of famine.” The verb means to sustain, supply, provide for. Joseph will use it again when he settles his family (47:12) and again after Jacob’s death, when his frightened brothers need reassurance: “I will nourish you, and your little ones” (50:21). The boy who was stripped and sold now undertakes to feed the father who sent him to Shechem and the brothers who sold him at Dothan.

The alternative is stark: “lest thou, and thy household, and all that thou hast, come to poverty.” Five more years of failed harvests would strip any herdsman of everything. Joseph’s offer is not sentimental. It answers a real and pressing need with real provision, and it shows that his forgiveness has substance. Love that speaks kindly but offers nothing is thin. John urges believers to love “in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18), and Joseph’s pardon comes with bread.

Behind Joseph’s care stands the care of God. The psalmist says the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, “to deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine” (Psalm 33:18-19). God kept his promise to Jacob’s family by placing one of their own at the granaries of Egypt years before the drought began. Providence often works through ordinary means such as storehouses, administrators, and a brother’s willing hands.

wordNotes.term: וְכִלְכַּלְתִּי (vekhilkalti) — and I will nourish
wordNotes.explanation: From kul, in an intensive form meaning to sustain or supply with food. Joseph uses the same verb in 47:12 and 50:21. Naomi’s neighbours call Ruth’s son “a nourisher of thine old age” (Ruth 4:15), and the ravens and the widow are commanded to “sustain” Elijah (1 Kings 17:9). The word speaks of steady, practical provision.

wordNotes.term: פֶּן־תִּוָּרֵשׁ (pen-tivvaresh) — lest thou come to poverty
wordNotes.explanation: A passive form of yarash, “to possess,” meaning to be dispossessed, reduced to want. Proverbs uses the same form for the sluggard who loves sleep and comes to poverty (Proverbs 20:13) and for the drunkard and glutton (Proverbs 23:21). Here the threat comes not from idleness but from famine.

verses.bibleText: And, behold, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth that speaketh unto you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers are still struggling to take in what they are hearing, so Joseph appeals to what they can see: “your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth that speaketh unto you.” His face, his voice, and his speech in their own tongue are the evidence. The man who had addressed them through an interpreter (42:23) now speaks to them directly.

Benjamin is named separately. He had no part in the sale, and his word would carry special weight with Jacob, who might well doubt the ten after their earlier deception. The father will need witnesses whose testimony he can trust, and Benjamin is the one son who never lied to him about Joseph.

The repeated stress on seeing and hearing also shows how deep the damage of the old lie went. Trust within this family had been broken for more than two decades, and it would not be restored by a single announcement. Joseph supplies every kind of proof he can: his face, his voice, his language, the witness of the innocent brother, and soon the wagons and gifts. Truth has to be made credible where falsehood once ruled, and Joseph patiently gives his brothers what they will need to persuade their father.

The New Testament also builds its message on eyewitness testimony. John speaks of what “we have seen with our eyes … and our hands have handled” (1 John 1:1), and Peter insists that the apostles “were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1:16).

wordNotes.term: פִּי הַמְדַבֵּר (pi hamdabber) — my mouth that speaketh
wordNotes.explanation: Joseph points to his own mouth as proof that no go-between stands in the way. Earlier “he spake unto them by an interpreter” (42:23). The LORD described his relationship with Moses as speaking “mouth to mouth” (Numbers 12:8), and Joseph’s brothers now hear him with the same directness.

verses.bibleText: And ye shall tell my father of all my glory in Egypt, and of all that ye have seen; and ye shall haste and bring down my father hither.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And ye shall tell my father of all my glory in Egypt, and of all that ye have seen.” This is not vanity. Jacob must be convinced on two counts: that Joseph is truly alive, and that he is able to provide for a whole clan through five years of famine. The account of Joseph’s honour and wealth serves both purposes. It also completes a story Jacob had heard long ago. When Joseph told of the sun, moon, and stars bowing to him, his father rebuked him, yet “observed the saying” (37:10-11). Now the brothers will report that the dream has come true, and that God, not Joseph’s ambition, brought it about (v. 9).

The verse ends as verse 9 began, with haste: “ye shall haste and bring down my father hither.” Joseph’s longing to see his father frames the whole speech. For all his power, the one thing Joseph cannot do is go to Canaan himself; his duties hold him in Egypt through the famine. So his glory must be carried by messengers, and his father must be brought to him.

Joseph’s glory was given to him for the sake of others; it became the means of their rescue. Jesus prayed that those the Father had given him might be with him to “behold my glory” (John 17:24). In both cases, glory is shown in order to draw loved ones home.

wordNotes.term: כְּבוֹדִי (kevodi) — my glory
wordNotes.explanation: Kavod comes from a root meaning “heavy” and can refer to wealth, weight of influence, or honour. Laban’s sons complained that Jacob had gained “all this glory” from their father’s flocks (31:1), where it means riches. Here it covers Joseph’s whole standing in Egypt: rank, wealth, and authority. Jesus speaks of the glory the Father gave him, which his people will one day see (John 17:24).

verses.bibleText: And he fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck, and wept; and Benjamin wept upon his neck.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s speech ends, and the embrace begins with Benjamin. “He fell upon his brother Benjamin’s neck, and wept; and Benjamin wept upon his neck.” They are Rachel’s only sons. Benjamin was born on the road to Ephrath as their mother died (35:16-19), and he was only a child when Joseph disappeared. Joseph had seen him across a banquet table (43:29-30) but had to hide his tears. Now nothing is hidden, and the weeping is mutual.

It is fitting that the embrace begins with Benjamin. He alone among the brothers had no share in the sale, and his innocence has been the hinge of the whole test: would the ten abandon Rachel’s second son as they had abandoned the first? They did not. Joseph first embraces the brother who never wronged him, and then, in the next verse, extends the same embrace to those who did.

The gesture of falling on the neck appears at the great reunions of Genesis and beyond. Esau ran to meet Jacob and fell on his neck (33:4), though that meeting left suspicion behind it. Joseph will fall on his father’s neck in Goshen (46:29). In the parable of Jesus, the father runs and falls on the neck of the returning son (Luke 15:20). In each case the embrace says what words cannot: the separation is over.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפֹּל עַל־צַוְּארֵי (vayyippol al-tsavve’rei) — he fell upon … neck
wordNotes.explanation: An idiom for a full, tearful embrace. It describes Esau’s welcome of Jacob (33:4) and Joseph’s meeting with his father (46:29). The same picture is drawn in the Greek of the parable of the prodigal son, where the father “fell on his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).

verses.bibleText: Moreover he kissed all his brethren, and wept upon them: and after that his brethren talked with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Moreover he kissed all his brethren, and wept upon them.” All of them: Reuben, who had argued against bloodshed but failed to rescue him; Simeon, whom Joseph had bound before their eyes (42:24); Judah, who proposed the sale; and the others who sat down to eat while he lay in the pit (37:25). The kiss is a sign of welcome and of peace, given by the injured brother before any of them has said a word. The initiative belongs entirely to Joseph.

“And after that his brethren talked with him.” This brief clause reverses the bitter note sounded at the start of the story. Then the brothers hated Joseph “and could not speak peaceably unto him” (37:4). Now, after twenty-two years, speech is restored. The narrator does not record what they said; the point is that the wall of silence has come down. Words between estranged people are often the first sign that peace has truly come.

Reconciliation is not finished in a single afternoon. Years later, after Jacob’s death, the brothers will fear that Joseph had only held back his revenge for their father’s sake, and Joseph will have to reassure them again (50:15-21). Forgiveness offered once must be trusted and lived out over time. The pattern here is the pattern of the gospel. God took the first step while we were still his enemies (Romans 5:10), and he has committed to his people “the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18). Those who have been forgiven are to forgive “even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you” (Ephesians 4:32).

wordNotes.term: דִּבְּרוּ אֶחָיו אִתּוֹ (dibberu echav itto) — his brethren talked with him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb dabar, “to speak,” links this verse to 37:4, where the brothers could not speak (dabbero) peaceably to Joseph. The story of estrangement began with the loss of speech and ends with its return. After Jacob’s death Joseph will again comfort his brothers and speak “kindly unto them,” literally “to their heart” (50:21).

verses.bibleText: And the fame thereof was heard in Pharaoh's house, saying, Joseph's brethren are come: and it pleased Pharaoh well, and his servants.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene moves from the closed room to the royal court. “The fame thereof was heard in Pharaoh’s house” takes up the language of verse 2, where the sound of Joseph’s weeping reached the same house. What the court now learns is the explanation: “Joseph’s brethren are come.” The vizier’s outburst was not a crisis of state but a family reunion.

The news “pleased Pharaoh well, and his servants.” The wording echoes 41:37, where Joseph’s plan for the years of plenty “was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants.” The man whose counsel saved Egypt has earned the gratitude of the king and his officials, and that gratitude now extends to his relatives.

This friendly welcome stands in sharp contrast to what comes later. A new king will arise “which knew not Joseph” (Exodus 1:8), and the descendants of these honoured guests will become slaves. For now, the blessing promised to Abraham is at work in both directions: Egypt has been blessed through Abraham’s seed, and Pharaoh blesses that seed in return (12:3). The king’s heart, like every heart, is in the hand of the LORD (Proverbs 21:1).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּיטַב בְּעֵינֵי פַרְעֹה (vayyitav be‘einei far‘oh) — it pleased Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “it was good in the eyes of Pharaoh.” The phrase repeats the reaction to Joseph’s counsel in 41:37, linking Pharaoh’s welcome of the family to his gratitude for Joseph’s service. The goodwill of one king would not outlast the generation that knew Joseph (Exodus 1:8), a reminder that human favour, however generous, is not the ground of God’s people’s security.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Say unto thy brethren, This do ye; lade your beasts, and go, get you unto the land of Canaan;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh gives the order through Joseph: “Say unto thy brethren, This do ye; lade your beasts, and go, get you unto the land of Canaan.” Joseph has already told his brothers to fetch their father, but now the instruction carries the king’s own authority. The family will come to Egypt as invited guests of the crown, not as refugees slipping across the border in search of grain.

The brothers have loaded their donkeys three times already: once on the first journey home with silver hidden in their sacks (42:26), once on the second journey before the cup was found (44:3), and once in despair when they turned back to the city under accusation (44:13). This time they load them for a journey of joy. Joseph stands between Pharaoh and his family as mediator, carrying the king’s goodwill to men who would never have gained an audience on their own.

There is quiet irony in the command “go, get you unto the land of Canaan.” The king of Egypt himself sends the sons of Israel back to the land of promise to fetch the patriarch. Generations later another Pharaoh will refuse to let Israel go, and God will have to break his grip. Here, in the days of Joseph, the throne of Egypt is made to serve the purpose of Abraham’s God without knowing it.

wordNotes.term: בְּעִירְכֶם (be‘irkhem) — your beasts
wordNotes.explanation: Be‘ir is a general word for livestock, especially pack and draught animals. The law uses it of a man’s beast that strays into another’s field (Exodus 22:5), and at Kadesh the people worry that they and their “beasts” will die of thirst (Numbers 20:4, 8). Here it refers to the donkeys that had carried the grain (44:3).

verses.bibleText: And take your father and your households, and come unto me: and I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and ye shall eat the fat of the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh’s invitation is generous to the point of extravagance: “take your father and your households, and come unto me: and I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and ye shall eat the fat of the land.” Joseph had promised Goshen and food; Pharaoh promises the best Egypt has. In a world where whole nations were coming to buy grain, the family of a Canaanite herdsman is offered the choicest portion.

“The fat of the land” means the richest yield, the best of the produce. The same word is used of the finest oil and wine and grain given to the priests (Numbers 18:12) and of “the finest of the wheat” God longed to give his people (Psalm 81:16). Pharaoh is offering abundance in the middle of famine. Later he will identify this best land with Goshen (47:6).

The offer carries an irony that later Israelites would feel keenly. The descendants of these guests would remember Egypt both as a house of bondage and as a place of food; in the wilderness they would complain about missing its fish and cucumbers (Numbers 11:5). Egypt could feed them, but it was never their inheritance. Joseph himself, in his final words, will insist that God would bring them up from Egypt to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (50:24-25). The patriarchs, as Hebrews puts it, desired “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Hebrews 11:16). The good of Egypt was a gift for a season of need. The promise remained elsewhere.

wordNotes.term: חֵלֶב הָאָרֶץ (chelev ha’arets) — the fat of the land
wordNotes.explanation: Chelev is literally fat, the richest part of an animal, which in Israel’s sacrifices was reserved for the LORD (Leviticus 3:16). By extension it means the best of anything: “the best of the oil, and all the best of the wine” (Numbers 18:12), or “the fat of kidneys of wheat” in Moses’ song (Deuteronomy 32:14). Pharaoh promises Joseph’s family the choicest produce of Egypt.

verses.bibleText: Now thou art commanded, this do ye; take you wagons out of the land of Egypt for your little ones, and for your wives, and bring your father, and come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now thou art commanded, this do ye; take you wagons out of the land of Egypt for your little ones, and for your wives, and bring your father, and come.” Pharaoh adds a practical provision. The journey from Hebron to the Delta was long and hard, and donkeys alone would not serve for small children, nursing mothers, and a man past 130 years of age (47:9). So Egypt provides wheeled vehicles.

The wagons matter more in the story than modern readers might expect. They are mentioned four times (vv. 19, 21, 27; 46:5). Carts of this kind were not part of ordinary life for herdsmen in Canaan’s hill country, and an Egyptian royal wagon was something no shepherd could buy or borrow. When the brothers arrive home, it will be the sight of these wagons, more than any words, that convinces Jacob his son is alive (v. 27).

Pharaoh’s attention to the weakest members of the family is striking. The children, the women, and the aged father are named specifically. The God who gathers the lambs in his arms and gently leads those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11) here works through a pagan king’s thoughtfulness to bring the whole household, down to its frailest member, safely to the place prepared for them.

wordNotes.term: עֲגָלוֹת (‘agalot) — wagons
wordNotes.explanation: Wheeled carts drawn by animals, used for carrying people or goods. The princes of Israel later brought six covered wagons for transporting the tabernacle (Numbers 7:3), and the Philistines sent the ark back on a new cart (1 Samuel 6:7). In Genesis these Egyptian wagons become a visible sign of Joseph’s power and care.

verses.bibleText: Also regard not your stuff; for the good of all the land of Egypt is your's.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Also regard not your stuff; for the good of all the land of Egypt is yours.” Literally, “let not your eye pity your vessels,” meaning: do not grieve over the household goods you must leave behind. Moving a large clan with tents, tools, pots, and furnishings over a long road was a heavy undertaking. Pharaoh tells them not to let such things hold them back, because everything they need will be supplied when they arrive. His generosity is that of a king repaying a debt: without Joseph there would be no “good of the land” left to give, and Pharaoh knows it.

Joseph had told them to bring “all that thou hast” (v. 10), referring especially to their flocks and herds, which they would need for their livelihood. Pharaoh’s word concerns the lesser possessions. In the end they did bring their goods with them (46:6), but the point stands: nothing they left behind could compare with what awaited them.

The principle reaches beyond this journey. Believers in the early church “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Hebrews 10:34). When God calls his people to move toward what he has prepared, attachment to what must be left behind should not keep them from going.

wordNotes.term: עֵינְכֶם אַל־תָּחֹס (‘einkhem al-tachos) — regard not (let not your eye pity)
wordNotes.explanation: The verb chus means to look on with pity or regret, to be reluctant to let go. It appears in the law’s repeated warning, “thine eye shall not pity” (Deuteronomy 19:13), and in God’s question to Jonah, who “had pity on the gourd” yet begrudged mercy to Nineveh (Jonah 4:10-11). Pharaoh tells the brothers not to grieve over possessions they leave behind.

verses.bibleText: And the children of Israel did so: and Joseph gave them wagons, according to the commandment of Pharaoh, and gave them provision for the way.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the children of Israel did so.” The phrase “children of Israel” is used here of Jacob’s sons acting together, but readers who know what comes later will hear the name of the nation. The family that goes down to Egypt will come up as a people.

Joseph carries out the king’s instructions to the letter: he gave them wagons “according to the commandment of Pharaoh,” literally “according to the mouth of Pharaoh.” He also gave them “provision for the way.” The phrase recalls the first visit, when Joseph secretly ordered their silver returned and gave them provisions for the journey (42:25). Then the gift was hidden, and it frightened them when they discovered it (42:28, 35). Now everything is given openly, in the light of reconciliation, and there is nothing to fear in the sacks. The phrase “according to the commandment of Pharaoh” also reflects Joseph’s integrity in office. Though he held the power to act as he pleased, he moved his family under the king’s explicit orders, giving no ground for any charge that he had used Egypt’s resources for private ends.

The contrast with Israel’s later departure from Egypt is worth noticing. When the nation finally left in haste, they had not prepared any “victual” for the road (Exodus 12:39), and God fed them with manna. In both cases provision for the way came from the hand of the one who called them.

wordNotes.term: צֵדָה לַדָּרֶךְ (tsedah ladderekh) — provision for the way
wordNotes.explanation: Tsedah means food for a journey. Joseph gave the same provision on the first visit (42:25). When Israel left Egypt in haste they had none prepared (Exodus 12:39), and the Gibeonites later pretended their dry, mouldy provisions came from a far country (Joshua 9:11-12). Here it signals Joseph’s open-handed care for the whole trip.

verses.bibleText: To all of them he gave each man changes of raiment; but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver, and five changes of raiment.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“To all of them he gave each man changes of raiment; but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver, and five changes of raiment.” The gifts are rich in themselves, for festal garments were a form of wealth in the ancient world, given as prizes and royal presents. But in the Joseph story clothing and silver carry a history.

The story has turned again and again on garments. Jacob gave Joseph a distinctive coat (37:3); his brothers stripped it from him (37:23), dipped it in goat’s blood, and used it to deceive their father (37:31-33). Potiphar’s wife held up Joseph’s garment as false evidence (39:12-18). Joseph changed his clothes to stand before Pharaoh and was then arrayed in fine linen (41:14, 42). The brothers tore their own clothes in anguish when the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack (44:13). Now the brother they stripped clothes them. Their torn garments are replaced with new ones by the hand they once laid on his robe.

The silver tells a similar story. Joseph was sold for twenty pieces of silver (37:28). Benjamin now receives three hundred. The money that once bought a brother’s slavery is answered by money given as a brother’s gift.

Once more Joseph gives Rachel’s other son more than the rest, just as he gave him five times as much at the feast (43:34). Favouritism toward a son of Rachel had once stirred murderous envy. That Joseph can now show it openly suggests his confidence that the old jealousy has been put to death. The brothers who offered themselves as slaves for Benjamin (44:16, 33) will not resent his gifts.

The returning son in Jesus’ parable is greeted with the command, “Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him” (Luke 15:22). In Scripture, a garment given by another often signals restored standing, and the prophet rejoices that God “hath clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10).

wordNotes.term: חֲלִפוֹת שְׂמָלֹת (chalifot semalot) — changes of raiment
wordNotes.explanation: Chalifah comes from a verb meaning “to change, replace,” so the phrase denotes sets of clothing, probably fine garments for special occasions. Such garments were valuable enough to serve as a wager (Judges 14:12-13) or as part of a royal gift, like the ten changes of raiment Naaman brought to Israel (2 Kings 5:5). Simlah, the word for garment here, is the same word used when Jacob tore his clothes in mourning for Joseph (37:34) and when the brothers tore theirs over Benjamin (44:13).

verses.bibleText: And to his father he sent after this manner; ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and meat for his father by the way.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s gifts to his father exceed even those to Benjamin: “ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and meat for his father by the way.” The “good things of Egypt” were probably fine goods and luxuries; the female donkeys carried staple foods, “meat” in the older English sense of food in general. Twenty pack animals made a caravan of plenty arriving at a famine-stricken camp. The number of gifts to Jacob doubles what Benjamin received in garments, as if Joseph wished to show that the father he had been parted from longest deserved the most.

The gifts served several purposes. They provided for Jacob’s journey, so that the old man would lack nothing on the road. They also served as evidence. Jacob might doubt his sons’ words, but he could not easily explain away twenty laden donkeys. There is a reversal here as well. On their second visit, the brothers had feared that Joseph was plotting to “take us for bondmen, and our asses” (43:18). Instead they return home with more donkeys than they took.

For twenty-two years Joseph could send nothing to his father. Now his honour toward him overflows. The commandment to honour father and mother (Exodus 20:12) belongs to the moral law God gave for all people, and Joseph keeps it here with open hands. Paul tells believers to learn to “requite their parents” by caring for them (1 Timothy 5:4). Joseph’s greatness in Egypt did not make him forget the old herdsman in Hebron; it gave him the means to bless him.

wordNotes.term: מִטּוּב מִצְרָיִם (mittuv mitsrayim) — of the good things of Egypt
wordNotes.explanation: Tuv means goodness and, by extension, good things or wealth. Abraham’s servant set out with “all the goods of his master” in his hand (24:10), and the returned exiles recalled how Israel once took houses “full of all goods” in Canaan (Nehemiah 9:25). The same root runs through Pharaoh’s promise of “the good of the land” (vv. 18, 20).

verses.bibleText: So he sent his brethren away, and they departed: and he said unto them, See that ye fall not out by the way.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So he sent his brethren away, and they departed: and he said unto them, See that ye fall not out by the way.” Joseph’s parting word shows how well he knows his brothers. On the long road home they would have to work out what to tell their father, and the truth about Dothan would have to come out. It would be easy for old accusations to surface. Reuben had already rounded on the others with “Spake I not unto you, saying, Do not sin against the child?” (42:22). Others might blame Judah for proposing the sale, or those who first wanted Joseph dead. Benjamin’s rich gifts might reopen old jealousies. Joseph forbids it.

The verb means to be agitated or stirred up, and it can describe both anger and fear. Here it most naturally warns against quarrelling and recrimination, which fits Joseph’s knowledge of his brothers and the shame that lay ahead of them. It could also be heard as reassurance that they need not fear being pursued again, as they had been after their last departure (44:4). The context favours the first sense, though both concerns would have been real.

The logic is plain. If the one they wronged has forgiven them, they have no right to go on accusing one another. Jesus taught the same in the parable of the servant who, forgiven a vast debt, would not forgive a small one: “Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” (Matthew 18:33). Paul urges believers to put away “all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour,” and to forgive one another as God in Christ has forgiven them (Ephesians 4:31-32). A family reconciled to its injured brother must also be reconciled within itself.

wordNotes.term: אַל־תִּרְגְּזוּ (al-tirgezu) — fall not out
wordNotes.explanation: Ragaz means to tremble or be stirred up, whether in fear or in anger. It describes the nations trembling at Israel’s deliverance (Exodus 15:14) and a fool who rages in argument (Proverbs 29:9). Psalm 4:4 says, “Stand in awe [ragaz], and sin not,” which Paul quotes from the Greek translation as “Be ye angry, and sin not” (Ephesians 4:26). Joseph warns his brothers against agitation that would turn into quarrelling.

verses.bibleText: And they went up out of Egypt, and came into the land of Canaan unto Jacob their father,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they went up out of Egypt, and came into the land of Canaan unto Jacob their father.” The verse is brief, but it marks the last of the brothers’ return journeys. The first time they came home with silver mysteriously in their sacks and Simeon left behind in prison (42:29-36). Long before that they had come home with a bloodstained coat and a lie (37:31-32). Now they come with all eleven brothers alive, with wagons and gifts, and with news that will overturn their father’s grief.

They also come with a confession to make. Jacob could not learn that Joseph was alive without learning how Joseph had come to Egypt. The narrator draws a veil over that conversation, but the truth could not stay hidden. The good news they carried would cost them their long-kept secret. Yet confession, painful as it was, would finally free them. A family that had lived for twenty-two years with a buried lie could now live in the open, and the father who had been deceived could at last know the truth about his sons and about God’s dealings with them.

The journey home to Hebron (37:14) is described as going “up,” as travel from Egypt to Canaan always is in Scripture, both because of the rising land and because Canaan is the land of promise.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּעֲלוּ (vayya‘alu) — and they went up
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘alah, “to go up,” is the regular term for travelling from Egypt to Canaan. Abram “went up out of Egypt” into the Negev (13:1). God later promised to bring Israel “up out of that land unto a good land and a large” (Exodus 3:8). The direction of travel points toward the land of promise.

verses.bibleText: And told him, saying, Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt. And Jacob's heart fainted, for he believed them not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The news comes out in a single breath: “Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt.” For twenty-two years Jacob had mourned a son he believed torn by wild beasts (37:33). He had refused to be comforted and had said he would go down to the grave mourning (37:35). Now in one sentence the dead son is alive, and not merely alive, but ruler of the greatest land in the world.

“And Jacob’s heart fainted, for he believed them not.” The verb means to grow numb or cold, to stop functioning. The shock is too great. Jacob’s heart stops short, as it were, and he cannot take in the words. There is a painful irony in his unbelief. When these same sons showed him a bloodied coat and lied, he believed them at once. Now that they speak the truth, he cannot believe them. Their past deception has damaged their credibility, and the news is simply too good to be true. “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick” (Proverbs 13:12), and a hope given up long ago is hard to take up again.

The disciples responded in much the same way when the women brought word of the resurrection: “their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not” (Luke 24:11). Even when the risen Jesus stood before them, “they yet believed not for joy, and wondered” (Luke 24:41). The announcement that the one mourned as dead is alive and reigning overwhelms people before it gladdens them. Jacob will need more than words before he can believe. He will need to see, and God, who knows the frame of his servants, will give him something to see.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּפָג לִבּוֹ (vayyafag libbo) — and his heart fainted
wordNotes.explanation: The verb pug means to grow numb, cold, or slack, to stop working. Habakkuk laments that “the law is slacked” (Habakkuk 1:4), and Lamentations calls on Zion to give itself no “rest” (literally, no numbness or ceasing) in weeping (Lamentations 2:18). Jacob’s heart goes numb with shock; he cannot respond to news he does not yet believe.

wordNotes.term: מֹשֵׁל (moshel) — governor
wordNotes.explanation: The same word Joseph used of himself in verse 8, “ruler throughout all the land of Egypt.” It answers once more the brothers’ scornful question about Joseph’s dreams (37:8). They now carry the news of his rule as good tidings rather than resenting it.

verses.bibleText: And they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said unto them: and when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob their father revived:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two things overcome Jacob’s unbelief. First, “they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said unto them.” The brothers repeat Joseph’s message, beginning, as he had told them, with God: God had sent Joseph ahead, God had made him lord of Egypt, and Joseph was calling his father to come (vv. 5-13). The words themselves carry Joseph’s voice. Second, Jacob “saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him.” Grain could be bought and donkeys could be hired, but no herdsman in Canaan could produce Egyptian royal wagons. They were proof that could be seen, and they were sent “to carry him,” an invitation addressed to Jacob personally.

Then “the spirit of Jacob their father revived.” The word for spirit, ruach, means breath, wind, and the vital energy of life. The phrase does not describe a separate being returning to Jacob’s body. It describes the whole man coming back to life: his strength, his will, and his hope. The same expression is used of Samson, who was dying of thirst until God opened a spring for him, and “his spirit came again, and he revived” (Judges 15:19), and of an Egyptian servant left starving in a field until David’s men fed him (1 Samuel 30:12). For twenty-two years Jacob had lived as a man waiting to die of grief. Now breath and vigour return to him.

The pattern of word and sign is familiar in Scripture. God often supports the word he speaks with something his people can see, out of kindness to slow and wounded faith. When Thomas would not believe without evidence, the risen Lord invited him to see and touch, and then pronounced a blessing on those who believe without seeing (John 20:27-29). The news that a son once lost is alive gives life to the one who hears it. The LORD dwells with the contrite “to revive the spirit of the humble” (Isaiah 57:15), and he “giveth power to the faint” (Isaiah 40:29).

wordNotes.term: וַתְּחִי רוּחַ יַעֲקֹב (vattechi ruach ya‘aqov) — the spirit of Jacob revived
wordNotes.explanation: Chayah means “to live” or “to come to life,” and ruach is breath or vital force. Together they describe renewed vitality in a living person, as with Samson after drinking (Judges 15:19) and the famished Egyptian after eating (1 Samuel 30:12). Isaiah promises that God will “revive the spirit of the humble” (Isaiah 57:15). The expression speaks of the whole person’s strength and hope returning.

verses.bibleText: And Israel said, It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel said.” The narrator changes the patriarch’s name at the moment of decision. Through the long years of grief he has mostly been called Jacob. Now, as he resolves to lead the whole family down to Egypt, he is called Israel, the name God gave him after the night of wrestling (32:28) and confirmed at Bethel (35:10). In Joseph’s story the name tends to appear when he acts as head of the covenant family. The heartbroken father rises again to the stature of the man God named a prince.

“It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive.” The single Hebrew word rav, “much, enough,” carries the force of full satisfaction. Jacob says nothing about Egypt’s riches, the wagons, or the promise of the fat of the land. What matters is that his son lives. The man who once bargained and struggled for possessions now wants only his son.

“I will go and see him before I die.” The verb expresses firm resolve. Jacob is about 130 years old (47:9) and speaks with sober realism about his death. He does not expect to live long, and he does not pretend otherwise; he will soon ask to be buried with his fathers (47:29-30). But before he dies, he will see Joseph. When at last he does, he will say, “Now let me die, since I have seen thy face” (46:30).

The scene anticipates the father in Jesus’ parable: “this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:24). It also recalls Abraham, who received Isaac back “in a figure” from the dead (Hebrews 11:19). Jacob received Joseph back from a death that existed only in his grief, yet the joy is the joy of resurrection, and it points to the day when God will restore to his people those they have truly lost. The next chapter shows Israel setting out, pausing at Beersheba, and receiving God’s own assurance for the journey (46:1-4).

wordNotes.term: רַב (rav) — it is enough
wordNotes.explanation: Rav means “much” or “abundant,” and used alone as an exclamation it means “enough!” Esau used it when he told Jacob, “I have enough” (33:9). Elijah used the same word in despair under the juniper tree: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life” (1 Kings 19:4). Jacob’s “enough” is the opposite: not weariness with life, but joy that his son lives.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can someone who has been badly wronged speak to the people who wronged them without either excusing the harm or seeking revenge?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Joseph forgives his repentant brothers because he sees that God overruled their sin to preserve life; their guilt is named, yet God’s saving purpose stands over it, and that vision makes reconciliation possible.
discussionQuestions: Why did Joseph send everyone out before revealing himself, and what does that say about how to handle another person’s sin?
Joseph says both “ye sold me” and “God did send me.” How do these two statements fit together without making God the author of sin?
Why does it matter that Joseph’s brothers had already confessed and changed before he spoke these words of comfort?
What signs in this chapter show that reconciliation has really taken place in the family?
Why did Jacob need both the words of Joseph and the sight of the wagons before his spirit revived?
commonMisunderstandings: Joseph’s words do not mean the brothers were innocent; he plainly says they sold him, and God’s overruling purpose does not cancel human responsibility.
Seeing God’s hand in suffering does not mean the wrong was good; it means God brought good out of what was evil (50:20).
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending nothing happened; Joseph names the sin before he lifts its weight.
Joseph’s comfort is not a pattern for telling sufferers that their pain was God’s plan; he speaks from the far side of his own suffering, about his own story.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the threefold “God sent me” at the centre, and keep it together with “ye sold me.” The God who rules history does not excuse sin, yet he overrules it for life, and the believer who sees this can forgive without denying the wrong.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The One whom we wronged has made himself known to us in Jesus Christ and invites us to come near; receive his forgiveness, stop punishing yourself for what he has pardoned, and extend the same mercy to those who have wronged you.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s providence and saving grace: the Lord overrules human sin to accomplish salvation, and the One who was rejected becomes the Saviour who forgives and provides for those who rejected him.
flow: Joseph’s brothers sold him out of envy, and their guilt haunted them for twenty-two years.
When Joseph revealed himself, they were terrified, for they stood before the one they had wronged.
Joseph named their sin but declared that God had sent him ahead to preserve life, and he forgave them.
In the same way Jesus was rejected and crucified by wicked hands, yet God used that very act to bring salvation, and the risen Christ offers repentance and forgiveness.
Come near to him, receive his pardon, and let it make you a forgiving person.
simpleIllustrations: A man receives a letter saying a son he buried in his heart decades ago is alive; he does not believe it until the son’s own vehicle pulls up at his door.
A judge who could pronounce sentence steps down from the bench, embraces the accused, and pays the debt himself.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you come near to the Saviour you have wronged, believe that he has forgiven you, and let his forgiveness flow through you to others?
cautions: Do not suggest that sin does not matter because God can use it; the brothers’ repentance came before Joseph’s comfort.
Do not tell people who are suffering abuse or injustice that God caused it; speak instead of God’s power to overrule and redeem.
Present Joseph as a type that points to Christ without turning every detail of the chapter into allegory.

reflectionQuestions: Is there a wrong I have done that still makes me afraid to come near someone, or to come near God?
Can I see God’s hand in a painful chapter of my life without pretending the wrong done to me was right?
Am I still punishing myself for a sin that God has forgiven?
Is there someone I need to forgive in a way that is concrete and generous, as Joseph did?
What evidence of God’s faithfulness has revived my spirit when I was slow to believe?
